MN202611_hk54szy19t.t:
Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student

Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.

It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.

"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.

But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.

When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.

"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."

Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death

Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.

She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September , according to the South African Police Service.

Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.

It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.

South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.

Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa

The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.

But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.

For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.

Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.

"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.

The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa

According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.

This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".

Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.

Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.

"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00

Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.

Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.

In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.

Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.

The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.

Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.

Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.

"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."

Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her

Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.

She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.

When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.

"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.

She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.

Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.

In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.

She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.

Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles

In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.

She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later .

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'

Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.

"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed

Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.

Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.

Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."

This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

MN202611_1e3b60042gu.t:
Maxine Dillion says she needed help to get through her to-do list

Maxine Dillion, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores.

Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it.

"I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media.

Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry.

Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.

Maxine, who earns £32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending £250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load" .

The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions.

Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present.

"If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.

Amanda says she and her husband made a conscious decision to spend more quality time with their family

With such companies also increasingly available in the US, another busy working mother, Amanda Sims Nichols in Austin, Texas, has also employed a firm to look after her life admin.

Amanda, who is a business consultant, has three children with her attorney husband, and decided to start paying for help with life admin after moving house, away from her family support network.

She pays $2,250 (£1,750) a month for 25 hours, and says she relishes offloading regular chores including the weekly food shop and clothes washing.

"Money cannot buy you everything, but it can buy you back some of your time," says the 45-year-old.

The company she uses, Queen of To Do, was founded by Kate Ginsberg in 2011. She says that interest has greatly increased since the pandemic.

The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers.

Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic.

Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small.

Some of the larger tasks her team has faced over the years include flying from Austin to New York City to buy a desperately needed Christmas gift, and finding a new wedding location for a client with just three days' notice due to an incoming hurricane.

Staff of life admin companies will do most jobs around the house for a client

Jess Baker, a UK chartered psychologist, says the appeal of such providers is understandable.

"Using a life PA, if you can afford one, takes the pressure off having to keep hundreds of to-dos swimming around your head, or on lists you might forget to look at," she says.

"Otherwise, the cognitive load can lead to feelings of being overwhelmed, excess worry and exhaustion."

While paying for help with such tasks may seem a luxury, for some people support with life's everyday trials is a lifeline.

Anna Allington sought help after her husband died. "My husband passed away. I was 47," she says.

"And the same week he passed away, I got leukaemia. There was a lot to sort out and I was very, very unwell."

Anna, now 51, still suffers the after-effects of her cancer. "I can't function executively like I used to," she says.

She pays £1,200 a month for 40 hours of help from Cheshire-based company Vi-Va. Her personal assistant helps her respond to emails, manage her diary and make travel plans and bookings.

"We meet twice a week on Zoom," says Anna, who lives in the Cotswolds, so they can go through all her tasks.

Many of us would love for someone else to do our laundry

Many more women than men use these companies.

Queen of To Do says just 20% of its clients are male, while only one of Life Laundry's 25 clients is a man.

Some of that disparity is likely due to mothers still looking after the lion's share of household admin, as studies continue to show.

However, Life Laundry's Forbes wonders if some men are too proud to ask for assistance.

"Men are struggling as well, but I think they're less likely to ask for help."

MN202611_12o0ve6trv0.t:
Ayana Bailey says she relies on her mum to go through the job application process with her

Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her.

"It's not like there's going to be a target on my back, but I'm just like, 'maybe they won't select me'," says Bailey, a part-time florist.

A British Dyslexia Association (BDA) survey of more than 1,200 working dyslexic adults found Bailey isn't alone - with 46% hiding their dyslexia at work.

Some 81% believe the condition adds to their work-related stress.

Bailey was diagnosed aged 11 and says she received good support at school, including mentoring, which helped her to understand her strengths and manage low self-esteem.

But the world of work has proved more challenging.

For Bailey, the application process is "daunting". She says she relies on her mum to go through it with her.

In interviews, Bailey says: "I just shut down. I completely forget who I am."

One way of coping, she says, is to have a little script, but she admits it doesn't always work.

Bailey, who studied film and wants to go into the creative arts, says that while dyslexia has sometimes made her feel anxious, it's also given her opportunities.

"I would definitely say my creativity and thinking outside the box [is my biggest strength]."

She says her dyslexia makes her a visual learner - able to imagine characters before seeing any written descriptions and helping her dream of becoming a casting director.

For nurse Lisa Daniels, her dyslexia meant leaving work more than an hour late most days just to finish the paperwork.

"I suppressed it. I was like 'Oh no, everything is fine. It's not affecting me.'" In reality, she says "it was majorly affecting me".

Daniels, 37, says a previous manager was dismissive of her request for adjustments.

"When I first started, they said, 'Oh they are babying some of these nurses' and I didn't have the confidence to challenge it."

Lisa Daniels says she has built up her resilience despite previous bad experiences at work

She says her suggestions of having more accessible fonts and colours on documents were not listened to.

Five years into her career, Daniels' colleague told her about a staff network on neurodiversity and her confidence grew, along with adjustments such as noise-cancelling headphones.

"I have that resilience that, despite the sometimes lack of support, I'm still gonna show up. I'm still gonna try."

Daniels says she's now recovered from her imposter syndrome.

Why I stopped hiding my dyslexia at work

Over half of people surveyed by the BDA say dyslexia makes them feel bad about themselves, while 39% have experienced bad mental health related to it.

The BDA is calling for workplaces to make reasonable adjustments for employees who need them, even without a diagnosis, and wants managers to be trained to understand and support dyslexic employees.

Its report finds dyslexic employees often have to put extra effort into work, finding their own ways to cope if systems, processes and communication are not accessible.

There are 3.3 million dyslexic adults currently in employment, estimates the BDA. Some told the report:

"I have to cope with little comments that are seen as banter about my spelling."

"My line manager is actually dyslexic and we happily talk about it. We share best practice and war stories."

"It would be nice to be seen as intellectual. Just because I cannot always write as well as others, doesn't mean I don't have the knowledge."

"I revealed my dyslexia quite early on in my employment… I do believe it was used as a stick to beat me with."

"I feel like I have got to do more, be more, show more... because I've got this deficit of being dyslexic".

Employment law solicitor Jenna Ide helped a client win a high-profile dyslexia discrimination case against Starbucks in 2016.

"Many dyslexic employees start a new job already struggling with low self-esteem," she says.

"That's especially true of dyslexics who are late-diagnosed and who may have spent years at school and in earlier jobs believing they just weren't clever enough.

"When an employer doesn't understand dyslexia, relies on inaccessible ways of working and doesn't offer support, it reinforces those feelings and can make people more reluctant to ask for help."

Kate Griggs, founder of UK charity Made By Dyslexia, agrees recruitment can still be a barrier, particularly when it is skewed toward written applications and timed tests.

"My advice to young dyslexics is simple: know your strengths, own them and talk about them with confidence. Ask for the support you need and different ways to show what you can do. Find the roles where those strengths are valued."

Lawyer Jenna Ide represented a client in a high-profile dyslexia discrimination case

Ellen Broomé, head of the British Dyslexia Association, said: "Dyslexic people should not have to work harder simply to have the same opportunities as their colleagues.

"Our research reveals the hidden cost many pay, spending additional time and energy compensating for workplaces that fail to understand or support them.

"This is not a question of ability, ambition or talent. It is about the barriers people face and the opportunities lost when workplaces fail to recognise and support different ways of thinking and working."

MN202611_9kvjjts6mv.t: Umunyamabanga mukuru wa OTAN, Mark Rutte, yatangaje ko uru runani rwiteguriye guhangana n’ico cose coza kibangamira umutekano w’ikirere c’ibihugu birugize, inyuma y’amakuru avuga ko Uburusiya bushobora kuba buriko burategura kurungika mu kirere ikigendajuru igifise ibirwanisho ruhonyanganda vy’ubumara (canke vya nikleyeri). Ibinyamakuru vyo mu Budagi vyatangaje ko amakuru y’igendereza yasangijwe ibihugu bigize OTAN yerekana ko Uburusiya bushobora kurungika ico kigendajuru mu misi 60 iri imbere. Amakuru yatangajwe n’ibinyamakuru vyo mu Budagi, NDR na WDR, hamwe n’ikinyamakuru Sueddeutsche Zeitung, yisunze amasoko yo mu gisirikare no mu nzego z’igendereza atashimye ko amazina yayo amenyekana avuga ko ico kigendajuru kizwi nka Sputnik-S, coba gifise umutwe ufise ibiturika vya nikleyeri ushobora guhungabanya canke gusambura ibindi bigendajuru bikoreshwa mw’itumatumanako no mu kugenzura ibikorwa bitandukanye kw’isi. Rutte yabwiye abanyamakuru i Berlin ko OTAN izobandanya gukingira “buri gace k’ubutaka bw’abayigize”, harimwo n’umutekano wo mu kirere. Arahumuriza kandi ko uru runani rufise uburyo butandukanye bwo kwivuna igitero ico ari co cose. Ku ruhande rw’Uburusiya, umuvugizi wa Kremlin (ibiro vy’umukuru w’igihugu), Dmitry Peskov, yamiriye kure ayo makuru, avuga ko ashingiye ku masoko atazwi, ubuserukizi bw’Uburusiya i Berlin na bwo bukaba buvuga ko ayo makuru atagira ishingiro kandi ko ari ugushikuza. Umukuru wa reta y’Ubudagi, Friedrich Merz, ntiyemeje canke ngo ahakane ayo makuru, ariko yavuze ko yerekana urugero rw’ukuntu Uburusiya bushobora gutuma ibintu vyunyuka. Hagati aho, umukuru w’ikigo ca Buraya gijejwe ikirere (ESA), Josef Aschbacher, yavuze ko gushira ibirwanisho vya nikleyeri mu kirere vyoba ari “ikintu giteye ubwoba kuruta ibindi vyose.” Aya makuru yongeye kuvyura impari zijanye n’iyubahirizwa ry’Amasezerano yo mu 1967 abuza kurungika ibirwanisho ruhonyanganda vy’ubumara mu kirere. Mu 2024, Amerika na yo yari yagirije Uburusiya ko bwariko buhingura ikirwanisho ca nikleyeri co gusambura ibindi bigendajuru, ariko bwarabihakanye. Ayandi makuru ushobora gusoma: Uburusiya buriko buhingura ikirwanisho ‘giteye ubwoba’ gisambura ibigendajuru – bivugwa na Amerika Uburusiya bwatangaje ko bwagerageje igisasu cya misile kirimbuzi kivuduka kurusha ijwi

MN202611_263j28ljj2.t:
Minisitiri w’Imari n’Igenamigambi, Yusuf Murangwa, yatangaje ko ivugurura ririmo gukorwa mu mikorere y’Umurenge SACCO rimaze gutanga umusaruro, aho igipimo cy’inguzanyo zitishyurwa neza cyagabanutse kikava kuri 9% kikagera kuri 3%.

Yabigarutseho ku wa 23 Ugushyingo 2026, ubwo yitabaga Komisiyo ihoraho y’Inteko Ishinga Amategeko ishinzwe Ubukungu n’Ubucuruzi, kugira ngo asubize ibibazo by’abadepite ku ivugurura ririmo gukorwa mu mikorere y’Umurenge SACCO.

Iri vugurura riri mu rwego rwo guhindura imikorere y’izi koperative zo kwizigama no kugurizanya, hagamijwe kuzinoza no kuzongerera ubushobozi kugira ngo zirusheho gutanga serivisi z’imari zinoze ku banyamuryango bazo.

Imwe mu mpinduka ziri muri iri vugurura ni uguhuza Umurenge SACCO zo mu mirenge zigakorera hamwe ku rwego rw’Akarere. Ibi bigamije kunoza imikorere yazo, koroshya imiyoborere no gutuma serivisi zihabwa abanyamuryango zirushaho kuba nziza.

Guhuza izi SACCO kandi biri mu ngamba zigamije koroshya uburyo abaturage bagerwaho na serivisi z’imari, guteza imbere ikoreshwa ry’ikoranabuhanga no kurushaho kurinda ubwizigame bw’abanyamuryango.

Ati “Imirenge SACCO ifite uruhare mu gufasha abaturage kwizigamira no kubona inguzanyo zo gukoresha mu bikorwa bitandukanye. Ni yo mpamvu kunoza imikorere yayo bifatwa nk'ingenzi mu gutuma abanyamuryango barushaho kugirira icyizere izi koperative no kuzigirira akamaro”.

Minisitiri Murangwa yavuze ko kugeza ubu inguzanyo Umurenge SACCO imaze gutanga zifite agaciro ka miliyari 200 z’amafaranga y’u Rwanda. Yagaragaje ko muri icyo gihe igipimo cy’inguzanyo zitishyurwa neza cyagabanutse kikava kuri 9% kikagera kuri 3%.

Kugabanuka kw’iki gipimo ni kimwe mu bimenyetso by’uko hari intambwe imaze guterwa mu kunoza imicungire y’inguzanyo zitangwa n’izi SACCO. Iyo inguzanyo zitishyuwe uko bikwiye, bishobora kugira ingaruka ku bushobozi bw’ikigo cy’imari bwo gukomeza gutanga izindi nguzanyo no gufasha abandi banyamuryango.

Nubwo igipimo cy’inguzanyo zitishyurwa neza cyagabanutse, Minisitiri Murangwa yagaragaje ko hakiri imbogamizi zigomba gukemurwa kugira ngo ivugurura rigere ku musaruro urambye.

Mu byo yavuze ko bikwiye gukomeza kunozwa harimo imikorere y’izi SACCO, kongerera ubushobozi abakozi n’abayobozi bazo ndetse no kurushaho kunoza serivisi zihabwa abanyamuryango.

Ati“Kongerera ubushobozi abakozi n’abayobozi ni ingenzi kugira ngo bashobore gucunga neza umutungo w’abanyamuryango, gutanga inguzanyo mu buryo buboneye no gukurikirana uko zisubizwa. Ni na byo bifasha izi koperative gukora kinyamwuga no kurushaho kugira imikorere inoze”.

Ku rundi ruhande, Minisitiri Murangwa yavuze ko kunoza serivisi zihabwa abanyamuryango bisaba ko izi SACCO zirushaho kwita ku byo bakeneye, koroshya uburyo babonamo serivisi no gukoresha ikoranabuhanga mu mikorere yazo.

Minisitiri yagaraje ko iri vugurura risaba gukomeza kunoza imikorere kugira ngo Imurenge SACCO irusheho kuba ibigo by’imari bifite ubushobozi bwo gucunga neza ubwizigame bw’abaturage, gutanga inguzanyo no gutanga serivisi zinoze ku banyamuryango bazo.

Minisitiri Murangwa yagaragaje ko nubwo hari umusaruro umaze kuboneka, hakiri urugendo rwo gukomeza kunoza imikorere y’izi SACCO, kongerera ubushobozi abazicunga no kurushaho guteza imbere serivisi zihabwa abaturage.

MN202611_wxlziskiwi.t:
Umushinga w’itegeko rigenga ibidukikije n’ihinduka ry’ibihe uteganya ko ibikorwa cyangwa imishinga ishobora kwangiza ibidukikije bizajya bisabwa gutanga ingwate yo kubisana, kugira ngo hirindwe ko ahangijwe n’ibikorwa by’abantu hasigara harangiritse burundu.

Byatangajwe na Minisitiri w’Ibidukikije Dr Bernadette Arakwiye kuri uyu wa mbere tariki 23 Ugushyingo 2026 ageza umushinga w’itegeko rigenga ibidukikije n’ihinduka ry’ibihe mu Rwanda ku Nteko Ishinga Amategeko Umutwe w’Abadepite.

Minisitiri Arakwiye yavuze ko muri uyu mushinga w’itegeko harimo ingingo zigamije gukumira iyangirika ry’ibidukikije no gushyiraho uburyo bwo kubisana nyuma y’uko imishinga cyangwa ibikorwa birangiye. Umushinga w’itegeko ushimangira ko hagomba kwitabwa ku nyungu z’abaturage batuye hafi y’aho ibyo bikorwa bikorerwa.

Minisitiri asobanura ko uyu mushinga ugaragaza ko Iteka rya Minisitiri ari ryo rizagena ibikorwa cyangwa imishinga bizajya bisabwa gutanga iyo ngwate, uburyo agaciro kayo kazabarwa n’uko kazajya gahuzwa n’igihe.

Iyi ngwate izaba igamije gutuma abafite imishinga bashyira mu igenamigambi ryabo amafaranga azifashishwa mu gusana ibidukikije igihe ibikorwa byabo birangiye.

Umushinga kandi uteganya ko uburenganzira bwo gusaba gusubizwa ingwate yo gusana ibidukikije buzajya burangira mu gihe cy’amezi atandatu uhereye igihe byemejwe ko ibikorwa byarangiye.

Izi ngingo ziri mu ngamba zigamije kurinda ko imishinga y’iterambere isiga yangije ibidukikije, ahubwo ko abayishyira mu bikorwa bazajya bagira uruhare mu gusana ahangijwe.

MN202611_42vafmo6wg.t:
Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space

Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.

Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".

The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".

Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.

"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".

"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.

A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".

Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation .

"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

Saurav Das said that he was supposed to deliver a series of lectures in the UK

A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.

Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".

It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.

Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests , said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.

He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.

"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.

A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.

Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.

"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.

Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.

In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.

The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.

There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.

In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.

In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.
